claims.text: Controlled titanium surface enrichment will improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components.
Diffusion treatment or thin-film deposition can produce a controlled nanoscale Ti-enriched layer on the component surface.
Titanium surface enrichment will form a stable Ti-rich interfacial layer during exposure to molten aluminum.
The Ti-rich layer may form stable TiB2 or TiO2.
TiB2 or TiO2 in the interfacial layer will remain intact during high-temperature exposure.
The Ti-rich interfacial layer will inhibit aluminum penetration into the boride substrate.
The Ti-enriched layer acts as a diffusion barrier that limits interdiffusion between the boride substrate and molten aluminum.
Limiting interdiffusion between the substrate and molten aluminum reduces the corrosion rate.
Titanium additions have produced similar corrosion-resistance benefits in related alloy systems.
Titanium can enhance corrosion resistance by stabilizing surface phases.
Ti-treated components will have lower corrosion depth than untreated boride-based components under comparable molten-aluminum exposure.
Ti-treated components will exhibit less interfacial degradation than untreated components.
Titanium surface enrichment may extend component service life by approximately 20–30% under similar conditions.
The protective effect depends on achieving an optimal titanium concentration and layer thickness.
A layer that is too thin or degrades during prolonged high-temperature exposure will provide diminished protection.
Changes in plating-bath chemistry or impurities may alter the stability of the Ti-rich barrier.
The treatment can remain effective at typical aluminum-plating bath temperatures and under thermal cycling if it resists long-term high-temperature diffusion.
